summary: SAKE: 2,154 author-written, four-option multiple-choice questions on software architecture knowledge, in eight categories derived from Bass et al. and the Gang of Four: three pattern families, quality attributes, architectural solutions/tactics, scalable practices, styles, and quantum. Eleven models were queried once via OpenRouter at temperature 0, zero-shot and five-shot. All models score 89-94%. Architectural Solutions is the weakest category (about 88%). Longer Architectural Solutions questions score lower, but question length is confounded with LLM-augmented wording.

claims.claim: Overall accuracy is high and tightly clustered (89.31-94.23%), so models are close to interchangeable on this knowledge
claims.evidence: Table 2. Single run, no CIs; most model gaps are 0.1-2 points, within sampling noise for 2,114 items. Descriptively solid as a saturation result.

claims.claim: Performance varies markedly across categories, revealing competency gaps central to professional practice
claims.evidence: Tables 3-4: Quality Attributes and Creational Patterns about 97%, Architectural Solutions about 88%. With about 250 items per category, CIs are roughly +/-4 points, so only the extreme gaps are clear. Calling 88% on textbook MCQs a 'competency gap central to practice' is overstated.

claims.claim: More context helps recall categories but hurts trade-off reasoning (Architectural Solutions)
claims.evidence: Table 5. 'Context length' is the question's word count, and §4.3 says longer questions were 'optionally enhanced via an LLM' (model unstated), so length is confounded with LLM-written augmentation. Architectural Solutions length bins hold about 60 items each; no significance tests.

claims.claim: Five-shot examples help large models and hurt smaller ones
claims.evidence: Table 2: changes of -4.21 to +0.66 points, single run, no tests.

claims.claim: Questions are expert-curated and validated (95.6% first-pass agreement)
claims.evidence: §4.3. The reviewers are the three authors; 'agreement' is an acceptance rate, not kappa; there is no external validation (the authors concede this in §7).

patterns.note: §2.1 notes that architectural knowledge is largely tacit and lost when architects leave. The benchmark tests textbook knowledge, not discovery of a project's own architecture or decisions.
Question answering without any codebase. Says nothing about exploring or answering questions over a real repository.
A new benchmark that is already near saturation for all eleven models at release.

methodology.sample: 2,154 MCQs (2,114 scored; 40 held out as five-shot exemplars)
methodology.baselines: None beyond model-to-model comparison; no human baseline
methodology.models: 11: Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus 4.x, DeepSeek v3.2, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, GPT 5.4 and Nano, Grok 4.1 Fast and 4.2, Mistral Small 4, Qwen3 235B
methodology.variance: Single run at temperature 0; no CIs or tests
methodology.contamination_controls: Questions are original (not copied from the books), but the public release invites future contamination; no canary string

standards.artifacts: Questions, evaluation scripts and results on an anonymous.4open.science link

biases.detail: MCQ recall is not architectural decision-making on a concrete system (conceded in §1 and §7).
One run per model and setting, so model rankings within 1-2 points are not meaningful.
Longer questions were extended by an unnamed LLM, which confounds the length analysis and may favour that model family.
The three authors wrote and cross-reviewed all items.

verdict_reason: An open, reasonably sized benchmark with released items. However, it is saturated at release, single-run, and validated only by its authors, and its context-length finding is confounded by LLM-augmented questions. The defensible takeaway is limited to 'frontier models score about 90-94% on textbook architecture MCQs, lowest on tactics and trade-offs'.
applicability: A weak signal for the discovery harness. Frontier models already know textbook architecture vocabulary, so a domain glossary of GoF or quality-attribute terms adds little. What developers who lack domain knowledge need is the team's own architecture decisions, ingestion data contracts and healthcare-content rules (P39), which this benchmark does not touch. The lower score on tactic and trade-off questions is a mild reason to keep human review on agent-proposed architecture changes across the ingestion repos.
